newsitem.title: USA: Calif. muni utilities says ISO depends on tax rule.
newsitem.headline: Calif. muni utilities says ISO depends on tax rule.

text.p: California's municipal utilities, which own about a third of the state's power transmission lines, do not plan on joining the independent system operator (ISO) unless U.S. tax rules are changed, utility officials said this week.

"We are still trying to convince the Treasury Department or the IRS (Internal Revenue Service) to issue regulations," said Jerry Jordan, executive director of the California Municipal Utilities Association.
As part of plans to deregulate the state's electric utility industry, California will establish as of January 1 a centralized operator for the state's power lines.
But municipal utilities are worried participation in the ISO could endanger the tax-exempt status of their bonds.

The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) intends to recommend participation to the City Council, but only after final word from Treasury or the IRS on tax consequences, said Eric Tharp, assistant manager of government affairs at the utility.
"Under the worst case scenario, bondholders could be charged with back taxes. We can't do that," Jordan said.
Under existing rules, municipal utilities are able to issue tax-exempt bonds as long as no more than $15 million or 10 percent of business operations fall under the private sector.
The ISO is expected to be considered a private use of the transmission assets.
State legislation passed last year requires California's investor-owned utilities to give up control of transmission lines to the ISO.

Municipal utilities, over which the state does not have jurisdiction, were given an incentive to join through provisions allowing them to recover "stranded" costs if they participate in the state plan.
Stranded costs are assets like nuclear power plant investments which are expected to be unprofitable under market competition.
Municipal utilities were given a "strong carrot" to join the ISO, but must first look out for bondholders, Jordan said.
Tharp at LADWP conceded there is a good chance go-ahead for the municipal utility to join the ISO is unlikely before the January launch.
He noted the federal authorities know whatever they rule will have national implications, as the industry is deregulated and utilities across the U.S. move to form ISOs.
Municipal utilities will also have to clear their participation with local governments, a process not known for speed.
In addition to UST and IRS rulings, there has been talk of Congressional action on the matter.
But questions of taxpayer subsidization of newly competitive electricity operations have complicated the debate.

Players such as the Edison Electric Institute, a trade group representing investor-owned utilities, have argued that public power utilities should not have authority to issue tax-exempt bonds if they want to enter competitive markets.
"Municipal utilities own one of the three interstate transmission lines to the Northwest and substantial lines to the east," Jordan at the California Municipal association said.
"Other members of the ISO have a big stake in seeing that the munis are able to join," he said.

Mark Ziering, manager of the California Public Utilities Commission's energy reliability project, said the ISO will improve system reliability, but the absence of the munis will not endanger its success.
"Right now you have three (investor-owned) utilities dealing with all the munis. After January 1 you will have one entity dealing with all the munis," he noted.
